claim: In Louisiana the lien, privilege and mortgage for unpaid tax arises automatically when the tax is assessed or the return is filed, whichever comes first. The Secretary may record a notice of it at any time after the tax becomes due or the assessment is made, whether or not the tax is yet payable. LDR says it may file a lien without notice once the balance is due and in collection, if that is in the State's best interest. Neither the statute nor LDR's lien page sets a dollar threshold or a waiting period for recording.

value.arises: automatic on assessment or filing of return, whichever first
value.recordedNoticeTiming: any time after tax due or assessment made, regardless of whether then payable

sourceDate: statute text as served by legis.la.gov (La. R.S. 47:1577, Acts 2003 No. 878); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: R.S. 47:1577(A): the lien 'shall arise at the time the tax is assessed or at the time a return thereof is filed, whichever occurs first.' 47:1577(B): the secretary 'may cause notice of such lien, privilege, and mortgage to be recorded at any time after the tax becomes due or the assessment is made, and regardless of whether or not then payable.' LDR Tax Liens page (https://revenue.louisiana.gov/collections/collections-information/tax-liens/, 'Updated August 14, 2025'): 'Once a lien balance becomes due and is in the collection process, the Louisiana Department of Revenue may file a lien without notice at any time if it is in the State's best interest.'
uncertainty: Dollar threshold for recording a lien outside a payment plan: NOT FOUND. Number of days after a notice before recording: NOT FOUND (statute sets none). The $2,500 / 12-month figures apply to payment plans only (see lien-payment-plan).
designImplication: Model the Louisiana lien as existing from the moment of assessment, with recording as a separate discretionary event that can happen at any time once the balance is in collection. Recording should not wait on a fixed countdown.

claim: Louisiana has no notice of intent to lien. LDR's own lien page says it may file a lien without notice. LDR does say that before any collection action it sends a notice explaining the amount due and the options, and the installment form says the normal billing includes a 'Notice of Intent'. But no form number or day count ties that notice to a lien.
sourceDate: page 'Updated August 14, 2025'; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: LDR Tax Liens page: LDR 'may file a lien without notice at any time if it is in the State's best interest.' LDR 'Learn About Collection Actions' page (https://revenue.louisiana.gov/collections/collections-information/learn-about-collection-actions/, 'Updated July 08, 2026'): 'Before taking collection action, the Louisiana Department of Revenue (LDR) will issue a notice explaining the amount due, the reason for the liability, and your options.' Form R-19026 (8/25) (https://dam.ldr.la.gov/taxforms/19026-8-25-F.pdf): 'The normal billing process will continue. Part of that process is the issuance of a "Notice of Intent."' R.S. 47:1577(B) puts no notice requirement on recording.
uncertainty: A lien-specific notice name, form number and day count: NOT FOUND. The 'Notice of Intent' named on R-19026 is not identified by form number, and nothing shown ties it to lien filing. It may be the notice of intent to assess, which is a separate step. The general pre-collection notice on the collection-actions page does not say whether it covers lien recording, which the lien page says can happen without notice.
designImplication: For Louisiana, do not give the player a guaranteed lien warning. A lien can appear once the balance is in collection. Any warning should come from the ordinary assessment and collection notices.

claim: A Louisiana lien on immovable property is recorded with the parish recorder of mortgages in any parish where LDR believes the taxpayer owns immovable property. A lien on movables, including titled vehicles, is filed with a parish clerk of court, or the Orleans recorder of mortgages, for the Secretary of State's master index. All filing costs are charged to the taxpayer. By rule, the fee equals what the parish charges LDR, assessed per parish.

value.movableProperty: clerk of court of any parish (Orleans: recorder of mortgages), for the Secretary of State master index
value.feeAmount: equal to the amount the parish charges LDR, per parish

sourceDate: statute text as served by legis.la.gov (La. R.S. 47:1577); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: R.S. 47:1577(B)(1): notices on immovables 'shall be filed in the office of the parish recorder of mortgages of any parish wherein the secretary has reason to believe the tax debtor owns immovable property.' (B)(2)(a): notices on movables 'shall be filed with the clerk of court of any parish or in the case of Orleans Parish, with the recorder of mortgages ... for inclusion in the master index of information maintained by the secretary of state.' (B)(3): 'All costs associated with filing the notices provided for herein shall be assessed against the taxpayer.' LAC 61:I.5302(G), adopted rule LR 42 (Feb. 2016) (https://dam.ldr.la.gov/lawspolicies/Adopted%20Rule%20-%201602RUL037.pdf): fee 'determined according to the amount charged the department by the parish in which the lien is filed', and with multiple parishes 'the total charges per parish ... shall be assessed against the taxpayer.' LDR's lien page says the lien is 'recorded with one or more clerks of court.'
uncertainty: Dollar amount: NOT FOUND. It varies by parish recording fee, and no parish fee schedule was gathered.
designImplication: Add a Louisiana recording cost to the debt that scales with the number of parishes where the lien is filed. Use a parish-fee parameter, not a state constant.

claim: A Louisiana lien attaches to all of the debtor's property, rights to property and after-acquired property, both movable and immovable. It covers tax, penalty, interest and attorney fees. It lasts until the assessed liability, or a judgment on it, is satisfied or becomes unenforceable through lapse of time. The statute fetched gives no fixed lien term and no renewal procedure.

value.attachesTo: all property, rights to property and after-acquired property, movable and immovable
value.durationRule: until liability or judgment satisfied or unenforceable by lapse of time

sourceDate: statute text as served by legis.la.gov (La. R.S. 47:1577); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: R.S. 47:1577(A): 'any tax, penalty, interest, or attorney fee ... shall operate as a lien, privilege, and mortgage on all of the property, rights to property, or after-acquired property of the tax debtor, both movable and immovable' and 'shall continue ... until the liability for the amount assessed or a judgment against the tax debtor arising out of such liability is satisfied or becomes unenforceable by reason of lapse of time.'
uncertainty: Number of years the recorded inscription stays effective, and any reinscription or renewal rule for LDR liens: NOT FOUND. A web search turned up general Louisiana reinscription rules (10 years) and property-tax lien certificates (R.S. 47:2155, 7 years). Neither was confirmed to govern LDR income-tax liens, so neither is used. The collection prescription period was not researched.
designImplication: Tie the Louisiana lien's life to the debt's life, not to a fixed timer. Leave the inscription term as an open parameter until it is sourced.

claim: Once the tax, penalty and interest secured by a recorded lien are paid, the Secretary may authorize cancellation. To get the payoff figure, the taxpayer files Form R-19023 by email, and LDR normally answers in 4 to 5 business days. Cancellation fees and costs are charged to the taxpayer, at the parish's charge. Cancellation is also available by posting a surety bond of at least 1.5 times the debt. Partial releases are available too. Neither the statute nor LDR's pages give a deadline for issuing the release after payment, and none addresses a release for an erroneous filing.

value.taxpayerMustRequest: payoff must be requested via R-19023; whether release issues without a request: not stated

sourceDate: statute text as served by legis.la.gov (La. R.S. 47:1578, as amended through Acts 2015 No. 130); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: R.S. 47:1578(A): 'where the tax, penalty, or interest secured by a recorded lien ... have been paid, the secretary ... may authorize the cancellation thereof.' (B)(1): cancellation if the taxpayer furnishes a surety bond 'not less than one and one-half times the amount of the obligation due.' (D): 'All fees or costs associated with the cancellation or release ... shall be assessed against the taxpayer.' Form R-19023 (8/25) (https://dam.ldr.la.gov/taxforms/19023-8-25-F.pdf): 'Response time will normally be from 4 to 5 business days' and 'This request will not stop any applicable interest and/or penalties from accruing or stop any collection action.' LAC 61:I.5302(G) (adopted Feb. 2016): a fee for 'the cancellation of a lien' at the parish's charge.
uncertainty: Days from full payment to release: NOT FOUND. The 4-5 business days is the payoff-quote response, not the release. Whether LDR releases without being asked: NOT FOUND. Release for a lien filed in error: NOT FOUND. Note that the statute says 'may authorize', not 'shall'.
designImplication: In Louisiana, model release as a step the player starts (request payoff, pay, then cancellation) that adds a parish cancellation fee. Do not model an automatic release on a fixed timer.

claim: No Louisiana statute or LDR page found sets a procedure or time frame for disputing or correcting a lien filed in error. LDR's general collection guidance only tells taxpayers to contact LDR if they believe a notice or action was issued in error. Disputes over the underlying assessment go through the proposed-assessment and appeal process, which was not researched here.

value.genericInstruction: contact LDR if you believe the notice was issued in error

sourceDate: page 'Updated July 08, 2026'; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Collection-actions page: 'Contact LDR if you believe the notice was issued in error' and, for liens, 'Contact LDR if you need additional lien information.' R.S. 47:1578 (https://legis.la.gov/Legis/LawPrint.aspx?d=101281) covers cancellation on payment, bond or partial release, but has no erroneous-filing provision.
uncertainty: An erroneous-lien procedure and its days: NOT FOUND. Searched R.S. 47:1577, 47:1578, LAC 61:I.5302, and LDR's lien, collection-actions and assessment-notice pages.
designImplication: For Louisiana, route a wrongly filed lien through a generic 'contact the department' action with no guaranteed turnaround. Do not borrow another state's withdrawal certificate.

claim: LDR's individual income installment form says that, to protect the state's interest, a state tax lien may be filed if the tax due is over $2,500 and/or the payments run past 12 months. A plan does not stop the normal billing. If the taxpayer misses a payment, the whole balance becomes due and collection resumes. Nothing found says LDR releases or withholds an existing lien while a plan is current.
sourceDate: Form R-19026 revision 8/25; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: R-19026 (8/25): 'To protect the state's interest, a state tax lien may be filed if the tax due is greater than $2,500 and/or if payments exceed 12 months in duration.' Also: 'non-refundable installment agreement fee of $105', not required if Louisiana AGI is $25,000 or less, a '$60 reinstatement installment fee', and 'A down payment of 20 percent of the total amount due may be required.' On default, 'the total outstanding balance will be immediately due ... all collection actions will be reactivated.' LDR Payment Plans page (https://revenue.louisiana.gov/collections/collections-information/installment-agreements-payment-plans/, 'Updated July 13, 2026'): 'Submitting a request does not necessarily stop an enforcement action that has already begun.'
uncertainty: The reported $2,500 / 12-month rule is VERIFIED on LDR's own form. The wording is 'may be filed', so it is discretionary, not mandatory. Whether a lien is withheld below those thresholds, or released while a plan is current: NOT FOUND. The current LDR Payment Plans page does not repeat the $2,500 / 12-month language.
designImplication: For a Louisiana plan, roll for or allow a lien when the balance is over $2,500 or the plan runs past 12 months. Below both thresholds, lean toward no lien. Never release an existing lien just because a plan starts.

claim: LDR says recording makes the lien public record and secures the debt, and that a lien may affect the taxpayer's ability to sell, refinance or transfer property. By statute, a recorded lien takes priority over mortgagees, purchasers and others whose interests are perfected after recording. Against all other third parties it ranks from the assessment or return date. LDR also lists driver's license and hunting and fishing license suspension among its collection actions for some delinquent liabilities, but does not tie them to the lien.

namedEffects: may affect ability to sell, refinance, or transfer property
priority against later-perfected mortgagees/purchasers from recording; against other third parties from assessment/return date
separateLicenseActions: hunting and fishing license suspension or denial

sourceDate: page 'Updated July 08, 2026'; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Collection-actions page: 'A tax lien protects the State's legal interest in your property until your tax liability has been resolved. A lien may affect your ability to sell, refinance, or transfer property.' It also says 'Certain delinquent tax liabilities may result in the suspension of your Louisiana driver's license.' Tax Liens page: the lien 'is recorded with one or more clerks of court to make it public record and secure the debt.' R.S. 47:1577(C) (https://legis.la.gov/legis/LawPrint.aspx?d=101280): the lien is 'not valid against any mortgagee, purchaser, secured party, judgment lien creditor ... whose interest ... is perfected prior to the time notice ... is recorded' and 'shall affect the rights of all other third parties from the date the assessment is made or a return thereof is filed.'
uncertainty: Thresholds and conditions for license suspension were not researched, and it is not a lien effect. Credit effects were not researched, per the instructions.
designImplication: Have a recorded Louisiana lien block or complicate selling, refinancing or transferring property. Keep license suspension as a separate collection action with its own trigger.

claim: In Massachusetts the lien arises by statute when a person 'neglects or refuses to pay the same after demand'. It dates from when the assessment is made or deemed made. Against mortgagees, pledgees, purchasers and judgment creditors it is valid only once DOR files a notice. Collection activity, liens included, can start if any amount is still unpaid 10 days after the Statement of Account (the demand) and the assessment is not disputed. No dollar threshold for filing was found.

value.arises: after demand is unpaid; effective from assessment date

sourceDate: statute page undated (M.G.L. c. 62C, s. 50 as served by malegislature.gov); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: M.G.L. c. 62C s. 50(a): 'If any person liable to pay any tax neglects or refuses to pay the same after demand, the amount ... shall be a lien in favor of the commonwealth upon all property and rights to property' and 'The lien shall arise at the time the assessment is made or deemed to be made.' s. 50(b): not valid against mortgagee, pledgee, purchaser or judgment creditor 'until notice thereof has been filed by the commissioner.' DOR Notices and Bills page (https://www.mass.gov/info-details/dor-notices-and-bills, read via Internet Archive capture of 2026-05-17): the Statement of Account carries a Demand for Payment and 'a $30 demand penalty', and 'Collection activity can take place at this time if: Any amount remains unpaid 10 days after the Statement of Account is issued. You have not disputed the assessment.' AP 631 (https://www.mass.gov/administrative-procedure/ap-631-the-collection-process, dated 01/30/2026): 'To protect the Commonwealth's interests, the collector will file a Notice of Massachusetts Tax Lien.'
uncertainty: Dollar threshold for filing a notice of lien: NOT FOUND. mass.gov returned HTTP 403 to direct fetches, so the DOR pages were read from Internet Archive captures (2026-05 and 2026-06). They are official DOR text, but not today's live copy.
designImplication: For Massachusetts, start the lien clock at the unpaid demand, the Statement of Account. Allow filing once 10 days pass without payment or dispute, and keep the effective date at the assessment date.

claim: Massachusetts DOR has no notice of intent to lien. The notices before collection are the Notice of Assessment, then the Statement of Account (the demand, with collection possible after 10 days), then a Notice of Collection or Final Notice from the Collections Bureau. That last notice says collection activity, which includes liens, may follow. DOR notifies the taxpayer in writing after a Notice of Massachusetts Tax Lien has been filed.

precedingNotices: Notice of Collection or Final Notice
value.postFilingNotice: written notice of amount and places recorded

sourceDate: AP 631 dated 01/30/2026 (read via Internet Archive capture of 2026-06-07); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: AP 631 General Provisions: 'When an account has been transferred to Collections, a Notice of Collection or a Final Notice will be issued showing the amount of the tax owed and indicating the date by which full payment must be made.' AP 631.1: 'When the Notice of Massachusetts Tax Lien is filed, the taxpayer will be notified in writing of the amount of the lien and the places it has been recorded.' DOR Notices and Bills page: a Final Notice is issued when earlier bills went unanswered, and 'Collection activity consists of: Bank Levy Wage Levy Liens Suspended licenses'.
uncertainty: A lien-specific notice of intent, its form number and its days: NOT FOUND. Form or notice numbers for the Final Notice and Notice of Collection: NOT FOUND. The Final Notice payment date is set per notice; no fixed day count was found.
designImplication: For Massachusetts, warn through the Final Notice. Treat the lien as able to follow without its own countdown, and send a post-filing notice that says where it was recorded.

claim: Massachusetts DOR records a Notice of Massachusetts Tax Lien with the Secretary of State in Boston, which is the UCC filing office for personal property. It also records at the registry of deeds of the county where the taxpayer lives and/or owns real property. By statute, filing a lien notice, waiver or release is recorded 'without payment of any fee'. No recording fee charged to the taxpayer was found.

value.realProperty: county registry of deeds where property is situated
value.personalProperty: UCC Article 9 filing office (Secretary of State, Boston)
value.feeBasis: statute: received and recorded without payment of any fee

sourceDate: statute page undated; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: M.G.L. c. 62C s. 50(b)(1)-(2): notice filed for real property 'in the registry of deeds of the county where such property is situated' and for personal property 'in the filing office in which the filing of a financing statement would perfect, under Article 9 of chapter 106 ...' and 'The filing of a notice of any such lien or of a waiver or release of any such lien shall be received and registered or recorded without payment of any fee.' 830 CMR 62C.50.1(4)(c) (https://www.mass.gov/regulations/830-CMR-62c501-lien-on-property, amended 2/24/17, via Internet Archive capture of 2026-09-10) repeats the no-fee rule. AP 631.1: 'recorded at the Secretary of State's Office in Boston and at the Registry of Deeds of the county in which the taxpayer resides and/or where any real property is situated.'
uncertainty: The statute exempts the filing from recording fees. No source says DOR passes any other cost to the taxpayer, so 0 is read from the statute, not from a DOR fee statement.
designImplication: For Massachusetts, add no recording fee to the debt. The lien's cost is its effect on property, not a charge.

claim: A Massachusetts lien attaches to all real and personal property and rights to property, including property acquired later. It reaches grantor-trust and disregarded-entity property for the owner's tax. It lasts 10 years from the assessment, or longer when IRC section 6322 allows. DOR may refile the notice during a one-year refiling window ending 30 days after the 10-year mark. A refiled lien ends at satisfaction or no later than 20 years from assessment, and each further refiling extends it another 10 years.

value.attachesTo: all real and personal property and rights to property, including after-acquired
value.from: date of assessment, deemed assessment or self-assessment
value.renewal: refile within the required refiling period (one-year period ending 30 days after 10 years from assessment)
value.refiledLienLimit: satisfaction or not later than 20 years from assessment; subsequent refilings add 10 years

sourceDate: 830 CMR 62C.50.1, promulgated 1/22/10, amended 2/24/17 (read via Internet Archive capture of 2026-09-10); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: 830 CMR 62C.50.1(3)(b): the lien 'shall continue to attach to all property and rights to property, including property acquired after the lien arises.' (5)(a): 'A refiled lien will terminate upon satisfaction of the outstanding liability, or not later than twenty years from the date when the assessment ... was made' and a lien 'again refiled in any subsequent required refiling period is extended for an additional ten years.' (5)(c): the required refiling period is 'the one-year period ending 30 days after the expiration of 10 years after the date of the assessment.' M.G.L. c. 62C s. 50(a) (https://malegislature.gov/Laws/GeneralLaws/PartI/TitleIX/Chapter62C/Section50): 'in full force and effect for: (i) a period of 10 years after the date of assessment ... or (ii) for such longer period ... as permitted by section 6322 of the Code.' AP 631.1: 'Tax liens will remain in effect for 10 years from the date of assessment or for a longer period if permitted by I.R.C. s. 6322.'
uncertainty: The regulation's 20-year cap language sits beside the statute's open-ended 'longer period' and successive 10-year refilings, and the two read somewhat inconsistently. Treat the outer limit as uncertain.
designImplication: For Massachusetts, run a 10-year lien timer from assessment, with an optional refile event near year 10 that extends it. Do not run it from the filing date.

claim: To get a Massachusetts lien released, the taxpayer pays the amount on the lien plus accrued interest and penalties. Payment by bank check, money order, certified check or attorney client-fund check gets an immediate release. Otherwise release ordinarily waits after the payment is credited: 30 days for a personal check (sooner with proof the check cleared), 20 days for ACH or debit card, 1 day for a credit card. DOR records the release itself and notifies the recording offices. If it was not released, the taxpayer may ask the Chief of the Collections Bureau. Recording a release costs nothing. The regulation also lets DOR revoke a release it issued erroneously.

value.requestIfNotReleased: Chief, Collections Bureau, PO Box 7021, Boston MA 02204

sourceDate: AP 631 dated 01/30/2026 (read via Internet Archive capture of 2026-06-07); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: AP 631.1.1: 'If the taxpayer wants an immediate release of the lien, payment must be made by bank check, personal money order, certified check, or attorney's Client Fund check.' Personal check: 'not released until 30 days after the date the payment is credited'. 'ACH or Debit card ... 20 days'. 'Credit card ... 1 day'. 'The Department of Revenue will make every effort to release tax liens by notifying the agencies where they have been recorded. If the taxpayer finds that the lien has not been released, he or she may request a release by contacting: Chief, Collections Bureau.' 'The Department of Revenue will record all releases of Massachusetts tax liens unless written instructions to the contrary ...' M.G.L. c. 62C s. 50(b): a release is recorded 'without payment of any fee.' 830 CMR 62C.50.1(8): DOR may revoke a release 'issued erroneously or improvidently.'
uncertainty: A release or withdrawal for a lien that DOR itself filed in error: NOT FOUND. The regulation covers only revoking an erroneous release. The day counts are 'ordinarily', not guarantees.
designImplication: For Massachusetts, release the lien automatically after payment, with the delay set by payment method (0, 1, 20 or 30 days). A cash-equivalent payment then becomes a real choice when the player needs a clean title quickly.

claim: No Massachusetts DOR procedure was found that is specific to a lien filed in error. What exists is this. Disputed amounts are generally not subject to enforcement while an abatement or appeal is pending (c. 62C s. 32(e), TIR 99-18). Taxpayers dispute an assessment with Form ABT, the Application for Abatement. A problem that normal channels fail to fix after two attempts can go to DOR's Problem Resolution Office. The Collections Bureau Chief handles release requests.

value.escalation: Problem Resolution Office after two unsuccessful attempts through normal channels

sourceDate: FAQ page undated (read via Internet Archive capture of 2026-06-10); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Collections FAQ: 'If you disagree with an assessment you may file a Form ABT- Application for Abatement with the DOR. In general, enforcement action will not take place on disputed amounts.' AP 631 (https://www.mass.gov/administrative-procedure/ap-631-the-collection-process): 'See TIR 99-18 for discussion of suspension of involuntary collection activities under G.L. c. 62C, s. 32(e) while the taxpayer disputes a tax amount.' AP 602, Problem Resolution Office (https://www.mass.gov/administrative-procedure/ap-602-problem-resolution-office), per a search-result summary: PRO handles cases where the taxpayer 'has made at least two prior attempts to resolve a problem through normal assistance channels.'
uncertainty: A procedure and day count for correcting or withdrawing a lien filed in error: NOT FOUND. AP 602 was seen only through a search-engine summary; the page itself was not fetched, because mass.gov returns 403. A search summary drawn from secondary sites described an 'informal appeal' and an ATB appeal of a lien itself. That is SECONDARY and unverified, so it is not used.
designImplication: For Massachusetts, let a player who disputes the assessment, via abatement, freeze enforcement on the disputed amount. Route a wrongly filed lien to a manual escalation path with no fixed turnaround.

claim: Massachusetts DOR offers a Lien Waiver Agreement, an installment plan of 12 months or less, as a way to avoid a lien. All outstanding returns must be filed first. Under an ordinary Payment Agreement the taxpayer 'may be subject to a lien' unless they set up a Lien Waiver Agreement or an accelerated schedule, depending on balance and term. Hardship status does not stop or release liens. No source says an existing lien is released when a plan starts.
sourceDate: FAQ page undated (read via Internet Archive capture of 2026-06-10); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Collections FAQ: 'How can I avoid a lien? You may pay the liability in full or enter into a Lien Waiver Agreement.' 'A Lien Waiver Agreement establishes an installment payment plan of 12 months or less. Before a Lien Waiver Agreement will be considered, you must file all outstanding returns.' 'Depending on the balance and the term of the Payment Agreement, you may also be subject to a lien.' 'Unless you establish a Lien Waiver Agreement, you may be subject to a lien.' Hardship 'DOES NOT ... Remove or stop the issuance of state tax liens.' AP 631.3 (https://www.mass.gov/administrative-procedure/ap-631-the-collection-process): 'Unless a taxpayer establishes an accelerated repayment schedule, the taxpayer may be subject to a lien' and a payment agreement 'extends the statute of limitations for the term of the payment agreement.'
uncertainty: The balance level that matters ('depending on the balance'): NOT FOUND. Whether a Lien Waiver Agreement releases a lien already filed: NOT FOUND.
designImplication: Give Massachusetts two plan types. A plan of 12 months or less suppresses lien filing. A longer plan leaves the lien possible, and a balance parameter can sit open until it is sourced.

claim: Massachusetts DOR says the tax lien is a public record that attaches to all the taxpayer's real and personal property and 'may prevent the sale or transfer of the property attached'. Once notice is filed, the lien is valid against later mortgagees, pledgees, purchasers and judgment creditors. On real property this requires the notice to name the record title holders. Separately, unpaid liabilities of $25,000 or more delinquent 6 months may go on DOR's public Tax Delinquents list, and DOR can suspend driver's licenses and professional licenses. Those are distinct collection actions, not lien effects.

namedEffects: may prevent sale or transfer of attached property
priority over later mortgagees/pledgees/purchasers/judgment creditors once notice filed

sourceDate: AP 631 dated 01/30/2026 (read via Internet Archive capture of 2026-06-07); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: AP 631.1: 'The tax lien is a public record and attaches to all of the taxpayer's real and personal property and may prevent the sale or transfer of the property attached.' AP 631.4: 'Unpaid liabilities of twenty-five thousand dollars or more may be subject to public disclosure' after 'a period of 6 months from the date the taxes were assessed' and if not resolved 'within 90 days of the notice'. Disclosure does not apply while a written payment agreement exists without default. M.G.L. c. 62C s. 50(a)-(b) (https://malegislature.gov/Laws/GeneralLaws/PartI/TitleIX/Chapter62C/Section50): validity against mortgagees and others only after notice is filed, and on real property only if the notice names the record title holders.
uncertainty: The public-disclosure list and license suspensions are separate collection tools with their own triggers; they are not consequences of the lien. Credit effects were not researched, per the instructions.
designImplication: Have a filed Massachusetts lien block property sale or transfer until it is released. Model the $25,000 public-disclosure list and license suspension as separate escalations, not lien side effects.

claim: North Carolina has no automatic tax lien on assessment. The lien comes into being only when NCDOR files a certificate of tax liability (CTL) and the clerk records it, and it runs from the recording date. NCDOR may file a CTL for any tax that is collectible under G.S. 105-241.22. That includes an amount shown due on a return and not paid, and an assessment final after a notice of collection or final determination. G.S. 105-242(c) sets no waiting period and no dollar threshold for a CTL. The 30-day wait in 105-242(a) applies to tax warrants (levy and sale).

value.lienArises: on recording of the certificate of tax liability

sourceDate: statute as served by ncleg.gov (G.S. 105-242, history through S.L. 2023-12); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: G.S. 105-242(c): 'The Department may file a certificate of tax liability to collect a tax that is owed by a taxpayer and is collectible under G.S. 105-241.22' and 'The tax stated on a certificate of tax liability is a lien on real and personal property from the date the certificate is recorded.' G.S. 105-242(a): 'If a taxpayer does not pay a tax within 30 days after it is collectible ... the Secretary may' issue warrants. G.S. 105-241.22 (https://www.ncleg.gov/EnactedLegislation/Statutes/HTML/BySection/Chapter_105/GS_105-241.22.html) lists when a tax is collectible, including '(1) When a taxpayer files a return showing an amount due ... and does not pay' and '(2) When the Department sends a notice of collection after a taxpayer does not file a timely request for a Departmental review of a proposed assessment.'
uncertainty: A dollar threshold for filing a CTL: NOT FOUND. A minimum wait between collectibility and the CTL: NOT FOUND (105-242(c) states none).
designImplication: For North Carolina, have no lien until a discrete 'CTL filed' event, which becomes possible as soon as the debt is collectible. The CTL's date then drives its 10-year timer.

claim: North Carolina has no separate notice of intent to file a CTL. The notice that comes first is the Notice of Collection (notice ID N0002203 or N0002204, or N0002401 when an amount shown due on a return was not paid in full). NCDOR sends it when the liability is final and collectible. It warns that without an immediate response NCDOR 'will begin forced collection actions', including 'Issuing certificates of tax liability (liens)', and may charge a 20% Collection Assistance Fee. That fee applies once a debt is 60 days overdue and not under an installment agreement.

claim: In North Carolina the tax on a recorded CTL is a lien on real and personal property from the recording date, and the CTL is enforceable as a judgment, with interest at the legal rate on the principal tax. It is enforceable for 10 years from recording, but not beyond the 10-year collection limit of G.S. 105-241.24. The period is tolled for absence from the state, death and estate administration, fraudulent-conveyance suits, insolvency proceedings, legal bars, and waiver. If the CTL is not satisfied within the period, the remaining liability is abated and NCDOR must cancel the certificate. The taxpayer may waive the period.

claim: In New Mexico the tax lien arises automatically by statute once the tax has been assessed and payment demanded and the person neglects or refuses to pay. Against purchasers, mortgagees and other creditors for value, the lien has no effect until the notice is filed. No statute or TRD page found sets a number of days that must pass after the demand before filing. The only dollar figure found is the general rule that the secretary assesses unassessed liabilities over $50.

NMSA 7-1-37(B), as amended by HB 218 (2025) (https://www.nmlegis.gov/Sessions/25%20Regular/final/HB0218.pdf, Section 32), says the lien 'shall arise at the time both assessment and demand, as provided in Section 7-1-17 NMSA 1978, have been made'. 7-1-37(C) says that against 'any mortgagee, pledgee, purchaser, judgment creditor ... the lien ... shall not be considered to have arisen or have any effect whatever until notice of the lien has been filed'. While an agreement is current, TRD does not pursue levy or injunction except in unusual circumstances. TRD says it 'does not actively seek collection' during a plan. On default, collection resumes without notice, and a taxpayer who defaults on a short-term plan may also be liened.

designImplication: For OR, model two stages: a silent statutory lien at assessment, then a distraint warrant that can issue 30 days after the notice and demand. Only the recorded warrant should bind buyers and lenders.

claim: Oregon's pre-warrant notice is the written 'Notice and Demand for Payment'. ORS 305.895 requires it to be mailed at least 30 days before a warrant issues. It must tell the taxpayer that a warrant may be issued and recorded even if they are compliant with an installment agreement and in contact with the department. It must also list alternatives that would prevent the warrant and the consequences, including garnishment and seizure. DOR describes it as the second request for full payment, after the Notice of Assessment. No form number was found.
sourceDate: ORS 2025 edition, ORS 305.895; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: ORS 305.895(2): 'At least 30 days before issuing a warrant for collection of any tax ... the department shall send the taxpayer ... a written notice and demand for payment. The notice shall: (a) Be sent by mail ... (b) Inform the taxpayer ... that, even if the taxpayer ... is compliant with an installment agreement ... and is in communication with the department, if the tax ... is not paid within 30 days after the date of the notice and demand for payment, a warrant may be issued and recorded ... (e) Include alternatives available to the taxpayer ... that would prevent issuance of the warrant ... (g) Inform the taxpayer ... of possible consequences ... including garnishment of wages or bank accounts and seizure and sale of real or personal property.' DOR collections page (https://www.oregon.gov/dor/programs/collections/pages/collections.aspx): 'Notice and Demand for Payment: This is the second request for full payment of taxes you owe'. A copy of the warrant itself must be mailed or delivered (ORS 314.430(1)).
uncertainty: The DOR form or letter number for the Notice and Demand is NOT FOUND. DOR's statement that the State Tax Lien letter 'is sent to the county' describes the recording, not a notice to the taxpayer.
designImplication: For OR, send a Notice and Demand and start a 30-day clock. When it runs out, a warrant may issue even if the player is on a plan, so the player cannot assume a plan protects them unless it is the ACH kind (see lien-payment-plan).

claim: An Oregon distraint warrant is recorded in the County Clerk Lien Record of any county. DOR may also file a UCC lien with the Secretary of State against business assets. State agencies are billed monthly by the county clerk at ordinary recording fees rather than paying up front. The warrant is satisfied only by paying the tax, penalties and interest plus all costs the agency incurred for recording, indexing or serving the warrant and its satisfaction. So the recording cost is passed to the taxpayer. The fee amount is set county by county, and DOR states none.

recordedWith: Oregon Secretary of State (UCC lien, business assets)
value.feeBasis: ORS 205.525(2): satisfaction requires 'all costs incurred by the agency in connection with recording, indexing or service'; fee is the county's ordinary document-recording fee (ORS 205.395)

establishes: ORS 314.430(2): 'the department may record the warrant in the County Clerk Lien Record of any county of this state.' ORS 205.395: the state agency 'shall not be required to pay the fee for that service in advance'. The clerk sends 'an itemized statement' monthly, and 'The fees that may be charged ... are those fees prescribed for recording documents.' ORS 205.525(2): 'An order or warrant may be satisfied by payment of the amount due ... any penalties or interest ... and all costs incurred by the agency in connection with recording, indexing or service of the order or warrant and the satisfaction thereof.' ORS 205.525(3): 'the cost of recording or indexing the release may be recovered in advance from the person seeking the release.' DOR lien page: 'We may also record a Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) lien with the Oregon Secretary of State.'
uncertainty: The dollar amount of the county recording fee is NOT FOUND; it varies by county and DOR does not state it. Sheriff fees on execution are added to the warrant liability (ORS 314.430(2)), but that concerns levy, not recording. Whether DOR in practice adds recording costs to every individual account is not stated on DOR's pages; it rests on the statute.
designImplication: In OR, add a small county recording cost to the player's payoff when a warrant is recorded, and again when the release is recorded. Leave it as a configurable number, not a sourced constant.

claim: The Oregon lien attaches to all property and rights to property, real or personal, including future assets. For businesses it reaches accounts receivable. Once recorded, the warrant has the effect of a circuit-court judgment and a judgment lien. Judgment remedies expire 10 years after entry. The agency may renew within 10 years of recording by recording a notice of renewal, which works as the one-time judgment extension: another 10 years. The underlying statutory lien continues until the liability is satisfied.

value.attachesTo: all property and rights to property, real and personal, including after-acquired assets; business accounts receivable
value.recordedWarrantEffect: judgment entered in circuit court register; judgment lien
value.renewal: notice of renewal recorded within 10 years (ORS 205.126(2)), effect of ORS 18.182 extension

establishes: ORS 205.125(2): 'From the date that an order or warrant is recorded in the County Clerk Lien Record, the order or warrant shall have the attributes and effect of a judgment ... including ... the creation of a judgment lien'. ORS 205.126(2): 'At any time within 10 years after the recording of an order or warrant, an agency ... may renew an order or warrant by recording a notice of renewal ... [which] has the attributes and effect of an extension of judgment remedies noted in the register under ORS 18.182'. ORS 18.180(3) (https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/ors/ors018.html): 'judgment remedies for a judgment in a civil action expire 10 years after the entry of the judgment.' ORS 18.182(5): extended remedies 'expire 10 years after the certificate of extension is filed. Judgment remedies ... may be extended only once'. ORS 314.417: the lien attaches to 'all property and rights to property' and continues 'until the liability ... is satisfied.' DOR lien page: 'Liens attach to all current and future assets'; 'The lien attaches to all business property ... including accounts receivable.' ORS 305.155(1): DOR shall cancel tax 'delinquent for seven or more years' only if also uncollectible and the taxpayer 'cannot be located or is dead'.
uncertainty: The 10 + 10 year figure is my reading of the chain ORS 205.125 to 205.126 to 18.180 and 18.182. DOR's own pages state no lien duration: NOT FOUND on DOR pages. Whether a warrant is treated as a 'civil action' judgment under 18.180(3) is inferred, not stated. The 7-year cancellation needs all four conditions, so it is not a general expiry.
designImplication: For OR, give a recorded warrant a 10-year life that DOR can renew once for 10 more. The lien reaches assets the player acquires later, so new purchases are encumbered too.

claim: After payment in full, Oregon DOR says it will 'send a lien release to the county where it is recorded within 30 days of payment in full.' The statute makes the issuing agency responsible for recording the satisfaction, so the taxpayer need not ask. Recording costs count toward satisfaction, and the cost of recording a release may be collected in advance from whoever seeks it. Partial releases of specific property and subordinations need a written request with documents. No erroneous-filing release with a time limit was found. ORS 305.140 lets DOR release real property from a warrant's 'cloud' or lien on request where a sale would not satisfy the tax, among other grounds.
sourceDate: DOR State tax liens page undated; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: DOR page: 'Lien Release: Pay your debt in full. We'll send a lien release to the county where it is recorded within 30 days of payment in full.' 'Partial Release: This removes a lien from a specific piece of property' (needs 'A written request', a title report and other documents). 'A "Subordination" allows other creditors to move ahead of us'. ORS 205.525(2) (https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/ors/ors205.html): 'When an order or warrant has been fully satisfied it shall be the responsibility of the agency ... to record a full satisfaction in each county'. 205.525(3): 'the cost of recording or indexing the release may be recovered in advance from the person seeking the release.' ORS 305.140 (https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/ors/ors305.html) and OAR 150-305-0050/0052 cover release of clouds and specific property.
uncertainty: A specific procedure and timeline for releasing a warrant recorded in error is NOT FOUND. The 30 days is DOR's stated practice, not a statute. The release recording fee amount is NOT FOUND (county-set). OAR 150-305-0050/0052 were read on Cornell LII and oregon.public.law (secondary hosts of the official OAR text).
designImplication: In OR, schedule the lien release up to 30 days after the player pays in full, so the lien stays visible for that window. Partial releases tied to a home sale should need an explicit request.

claim: No Oregon lien-specific dispute process was found. The notice and demand must name a DOR contact person and tell the taxpayer that 'questions or complaints concerning the warrant, other than liability for the underlying tax,' may go to that person. The tax itself is disputed through the assessment appeal: written objection or conference within 30 days, or the Tax Court Magistrate Division within 90 days of the notice of assessment. Unresolved problems can go to the Taxpayer Advocate. The ORS 305.140 release of a 'cloud' on title needs a written request with a title statement.

value.warrantComplaintChannel: person named on the Notice and Demand (ORS 305.895(2)(d))

sourceDate: ORS 2025 edition, ORS 305.895 and 305.140; DOR Taxpayer Bill of Rights page undated; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: ORS 305.895(2)(d): the notice must 'Contain the name, office mailing address and office telephone number of the person issuing the warrant and advise the taxpayer ... that questions or complaints concerning the warrant, other than liability for the underlying tax ... may be directed to that person.' DOR Taxpayer Bill of Rights page (https://www.oregon.gov/dor/Pages/taxpayer-bill-of-rights.aspx): 'If you disagree with the decision from the written objection or conference, or you didn't appeal within the 30-day appeal period, you may appeal to the Magistrate Division ... within 90 days after the date on the notice of assessment.' It also says: 'If you think you are not being treated fairly, or if you have a problem or complaint, please contact the Office of the Taxpayer Advocate'. OAR 150-305-0050 (Cornell LII copy, secondary host) sets out what a request for release of a warrant that is 'merely a cloud on the title' must contain.
uncertainty: A formal process and day limits for challenging a warrant or lien recorded in error (wrong person, already paid) are NOT FOUND. The 30-day objection window comes from DOR's rights page as summarized; the governing statute for it (ORS 305.265) was not read.
designImplication: For OR, route lien errors to a named DOR contact with no deadline. The tax itself can be contested only through the 30- and 90-day assessment appeals, so a late challenge leaves the lien in place.

claim: Oregon DOR offers payment plans of up to 36 months, and more with a Statement of Financial Condition. DOR says ACH (automatic debit) plans that pay the debt in full within 36 months 'prevent the automatic recording of a lien in county records'. It reserves the right to record one anyway to protect the State. The statute requires the pre-warrant notice to warn that a warrant may be issued and recorded even if the taxpayer is compliant with an installment agreement. No source says a lien already recorded is released while a plan is current. Plans do not require a lien.
sourceDate: DOR State tax liens and Payment Plans pages undated; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: DOR lien page: 'Automatic Clearing House (ACH) payment plans which pay your debt in full within 36 months prevent the automatic recording of a lien in county records. Note: We reserve the right to record a lien if we deem it necessary to protect the state's interest.' DOR Payment Plans page (https://www.oregon.gov/dor/programs/Collections/Pages/payment-plan.aspx): 'We offer payment plans up to 36 months'; 'Submit a Statement of Financial Condition form ... if you require more than 36 months to pay in full.' ORS 305.895(2)(b): the notice must say that 'even if the taxpayer ... is compliant with an installment agreement ... a warrant may be issued and recorded'.
uncertainty: Whether a non-ACH plan within 36 months also prevents automatic recording is NOT FOUND; DOR names only ACH plans. Whether a recorded lien is released or kept during a plan is NOT FOUND; no source says it is released. 'Plans do not require a lien' is inferred from the absence of any such requirement on DOR pages.
designImplication: In OR, make the payment method matter: an ACH plan paying in full within 36 months suppresses automatic lien recording, and other plans do not. Keep a small chance that DOR records a lien anyway.

claim: Oregon DOR calls the recorded lien 'the public notice of debt that attaches to your real property'. A recorded warrant has the effect of a court judgment and a judgment lien on title. Its priority against other real-property interests is that of a judgment recorded at the same moment. Purchasers in securities, retail sales, casual sales and some loans take free unless they have actual knowledge. Professional license suspension and the public Delinquent Taxpayers List (over $50,000) are DOR collection tools for unpaid debt, not effects of the lien itself.

namedEffects: public notice of debt attached to real property
effect of a judgment / judgment lien on title
priority equal to a judgment recorded at the same time

sourceDate: DOR Collections process page undated; ORS 2025 edition; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: DOR collections page: 'Filing a tax lien against your real property in the county lien record. This is the public notice of debt that attaches to your real property and your rights to the property.' The same page lists 'Professional license suspension' and 'Publicly posting your name ... on the department's Delinquent Taxpayers List if you owe over $50,000'. ORS 205.125(3) (https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/ors/ors205.html): the recorded warrant 'becomes a lien upon the title to and interest in property ... in the same manner as a judgment'. ORS 314.423(1) (https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/ors/ors314.html): the lien is subordinate to real-property interests 'to the same extent that a judgment recorded ... at the same time the warrant was recorded would be subordinate'. ORS 314.423(2) lists the transactions protected unless there was 'actual knowledge'.
uncertainty: A statutory block on title transfer is NOT FOUND. A lien on title in practice must be cleared or subordinated to sell or refinance; DOR's subordination text says this 'may make it easier to get a loan or mortgage refinanced'. License suspension follows from delinquency, not from the lien. Credit effects were deliberately not researched.
designImplication: In OR, a recorded warrant should appear as a public judgment-like encumbrance that a home sale or refinance must clear or subordinate. Keep license suspension and the $50,000 public list as separate triggers based on delinquency.

claim: For Pennsylvania personal income tax, the lien is created by statute when a person neglects or refuses to pay on the date the tax becomes collectible. It binds property only after the Department's certified copy has been entered and docketed by the county prothonotary, so it is filed, not self-executing. PIT regulations make an assessed tax collectible 90 days after the notice of assessment is mailed unless a petition for reassessment is filed. Collection follows later appeal stages too. DOR says it files liens 'when an individual or business has unpaid delinquent taxes.' No dollar threshold was found.
sourceDate: Tax Reform Code of 1971 s. 345 (72 P.S. 7345), PA General Assembly official text, last amended 1991; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: TRC s. 345(a): 'If any person liable to pay any tax neglects or refuses to pay the same on the date the tax becomes collectible, the amount of such tax, together with any costs that may accrue in addition thereto, shall be a lien in favor of the Commonwealth against the real and personal property of such person but only after such lien has been duly entered and docketed of record by the prothonotary of the county where such property is situated.' 61 Pa. Code 119.10(a)(3) (https://www.pacodeandbulletin.gov/Display/pacode?file=/secure/pacode/data/061/chapter119/s119.10.html): DOR will collect 'After 90 days from the date of mailing of a notice of assessment, unless a taxpayer has filed a petition for reassessment within 90 days'. Fiscal Code s. 1401 (72 P.S. 1401) separately makes state taxes 'a first lien ... from the date of settlement, assessment or determination, except as otherwise expressly provided by law under which the claim ... arises'. DOR liens page (https://www.pa.gov/agencies/revenue/tax-compliance/pa-tax-liens): 'The Department of Revenue files a lien with the county Prothonotary Office when an individual or business has unpaid delinquent taxes.'
uncertainty: No minimum balance or DOR waiting period after the tax becomes collectible was found: NOT FOUND. How Fiscal Code s. 1401 (lien from assessment) interacts with TRC s. 345 (lien only on docketing) for PIT is not settled by any source read. Section 345 appears to be the PIT-specific rule that 1401 defers to. 61 Pa. Code 119.10 dates from 1976; current statutory appeal periods may differ in detail.
designImplication: For PA, there is no lien until DOR docketing, which comes some time after the tax becomes collectible: 90 days after the assessment notice if no petition is filed. Model it as a discretionary DOR filing event, not as automatic at assessment.

claim: No Pennsylvania pre-filing notice of intent to lien was found. DOR says it mails a 'Certified Copy of Lien' letter after the lien is filed. The statute requires notice of the filing and its effect by certified mail at least 10 days before any execution on the lien, which is before a forced sale, not before filing. The earlier warning is the notice of assessment, with its 90-day appeal window for PIT.
sourceDate: DOR PA Tax Liens page undated; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: DOR page: 'The Department of Revenue will mail taxpayers a Certified Copy of Lien letter to notify them that a lien has been filed with the County Prothonotary's Office.' TRC s. 345(b) (https://www.palegis.us/statutes/unconsolidated/law-information/view-statute?txtType=PDF&SessYr=1971&SessInd=0&ActNum=0002.&chpt=3&subchpt=000.&sctn=45&subsctn=000.): 'Provided, That not less than ten days before issuance of any execution on the lien, notice of the filing and effect of the lien shall be sent by certified mail to the taxpayer'. REV-554 (04-25) (https://www.pa.gov/content/dam/copapwp-pagov/en/revenue/documents/formsandpublications/formsforindividuals/taxpayersrightsadvocate/documents/rev-554.pdf): 'The timeframe to appeal a personal income tax assessment is 90 days from the date issued on the notice.'
uncertainty: A pre-filing intent-to-lien notice, its form number and days are NOT FOUND. Secondary tax-relief sites mention 'final notice' letters, but they are not official and were not used. The Certified Copy of Lien letter's form number is NOT FOUND.
designImplication: For PA, the player learns of the lien after it is filed, by letter. The only advance warnings are the assessment notice and a 10-day certified notice before execution, so a PA lien should arrive as a surprise event.

claim: Pennsylvania DOR sends a certified copy of the lien to the prothonotary of the county where the taxpayer resides, does business or holds property. The prothonotary must docket and index it as a judgment and may not demand costs before docketing. The taxpayer bears the costs: the statutory lien amount includes 'any costs that may accrue', and the regulation conditions release on payment of 'prothonotary's costs and fees'. The dollar amount was not found and is county-set.
sourceDate: 61 Pa. Code 119.11; Pennsylvania Code site current through 56 Pa.B. 5370 (August 8, 2026); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: 61 Pa. Code 119.11(a)(1): 'The Department may forward for filing a certified copy of such lien, interest, penalties, additions, and prothonotary's costs and fees'. 119.11(b): 'No prothonotary shall require the payment of any costs or fees as a condition precedent to the filing and docketing of any such liens.' 119.11(e): release is available 'upon payment of all taxes due including interest, penalties, additions, and prothonotary's costs and fees'. TRC s. 345(a)-(b): the lien includes 'any costs that may accrue in addition thereto' and 'shall be indexed as judgments are now indexed.' DOR page: 'The department files liens in the county Prothonotary's Office where the taxpayer resides or does business.'
uncertainty: The prothonotary fee amount is NOT FOUND; it varies by county and DOR states none. Chapter 119 of 61 Pa. Code is in DOR's personal income tax regulations (its sections refer to 'taxes imposed by this article'). I identified it as PIT from the chapter structure; this was not separately confirmed.
designImplication: In PA, add the county prothonotary's costs to the player's payoff when a lien is docketed. Leave it as a configurable small amount, not a sourced figure.

claim: For Pennsylvania personal income tax, the lien reaches the taxpayer's real and personal property in the county where docketed. Stock in trade sold in the ordinary course is not bound until execution and levy. The PIT regulation says the lien continues five years from docketing and may be revived. The Fiscal Code allows revival for successive five-year periods by filing a suggestion of nonpayment and averment of default before expiry. Revived liens run until five years pass without revival.

value.excludes: stock of goods regularly sold in ordinary course, until writ of execution and levy
value.renewal: revival by suggestion of nonpayment and averment of default filed with prothonotary before expiry

sourceDate: 61 Pa. Code 119.11, Pennsylvania Code current through 56 Pa.B. 5370 (2026-08-08); Fiscal Code s. 1404 official text; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: 61 Pa. Code 119.11(a)(3): 'The lien shall continue for five years from the date of docketing and may be revived and continued by the Department in the manner now or hereafter provided by law.' Fiscal Code s. 1404 (72 P.S. 1404) (https://www.palegis.us/statutes/unconsolidated/law-information/view-statute?txtType=PDF&SessYr=1929&SessInd=0&ActNum=0176.&chpt=14&subchpt=000.&sctn=4&subsctn=000.): 'the Commonwealth may revive the same for a period of five years, and thereafter for successive periods of five years, by filing with the prothonotary a suggestion of nonpayment and an averment of default prior to the expiration thereof ... such lien ... shall continue in full force and effect until a period of five years has elapsed without the revival'. TRC s. 345(a)-(b): lien 'against the real and personal property'; 'said lien shall have no effect upon any stock of goods ... regularly sold ... in the ordinary course of business ... unless and until a writ of execution has been issued and a levy made'.
uncertainty: There is a conflict. TRC s. 345 (statute) says 'real and personal property', while 61 Pa. Code 119.11(a) (regulation) says 'real estate'. The statute should control, but this is not confirmed by any DOR statement. Fiscal Code s. 1404 revival applies 'Whenever the law under which the claim ... arises provides a time for the expiration of such lien'. TRC s. 345 itself states no expiry, so the five-year term rests on the regulation. Whether liens docketed in other counties need separate revival is NOT FOUND.
designImplication: For PA, use a five-year lien that DOR can keep reviving in five-year steps with no limit, effectively until paid. Missing a revival is the only way it lapses.

claim: Pennsylvania DOR says a lien is removed once it confirms the past-due liability is resolved, and 'The lien satisfaction process will start approximately 45 days after the resolution has occurred.' DOR then sends the taxpayer a lien satisfaction notice. To get a payoff figure the taxpayer files the Lien Payoff Request Form (REV-1038); DOR says to allow five business days for it. The regulation conditions release on payment of tax, interest, penalties, additions and prothonotary costs and fees, 'upon request of the taxpayer'. No separate release fee and no procedure for releasing an erroneous filing were found.

sourceDate: DOR PA Tax Liens page undated; REV-1038 (CM) 08-25; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: DOR page: 'A lien is removed when the department receives confirmation that the past-due liability has been resolved. The lien satisfaction process will start approximately 45 days after the resolution has occurred.' 'When a lien is satisfied, the department sends you a lien satisfaction notice.' 'complete the Lien Payoff Request Form (REV-1038)'. REV-1038 (https://www.pa.gov/content/dam/copapwp-pagov/en/revenue/documents/formsandpublications/otherforms/documents/rev-1038.pdf): 'Taxpayers or their representative must use this form to request a payoff balance to resolve a tax lien' and 'Please allow five business days before inquiring about the status'. 61 Pa. Code 119.11(e) (https://www.pacodeandbulletin.gov/Display/pacode?file=/secure/pacode/data/061/chapter119/s119.11.html): 'Prior to execution and upon payment of all taxes due including interest, penalties, additions, and prothonotary's costs and fees and upon request of the taxpayer, the Department may release the property subject to the lien.' claim: No Pennsylvania procedure specifically for a lien filed in error was found. The tax itself is disputed by petition to the DOR Board of Appeals: generally 60 days, but 90 days from the notice for a PIT assessment. Further appeal goes to the Board of Finance and Revenue and then Commonwealth Court within 30 days. The Office of Taxpayers' Rights Advocate helps PIT taxpayers whose issues normal procedures have not resolved. DOR directs lien questions to its Bureau of Compliance.
establishes: REV-554: 'To appeal any assessment or certain decisions of the department ... a taxpayer must file an appeal with the Board of Appeals. The general timeframe ... is 60 days from the mailing date of the notice.' 'The timeframe to appeal a personal income tax assessment is 90 days from the date issued on the notice.' A taxpayer 'may file with the Commonwealth Court of Pennsylvania within 30 days'. OTRA assists with 'An issue with, or action by, the Department of Revenue that has not been resolved by normal, established procedures' and 'An action ... that will cause a substantial hardship.' DOR liens page (https://www.pa.gov/agencies/revenue/tax-compliance/pa-tax-liens): 'If you have any questions about a notice or a lien, please contact the Department of Revenue's Bureau of Compliance at 717-425-2495, Ext. 91111.'
uncertainty: A lien-specific error-correction process, form or deadline is NOT FOUND. Whether filing a lien is itself an appealable 'decision' to the Board of Appeals is NOT FOUND. REV-554's wording on the PIT 90-day period sits between its Board of Appeals and Board of Finance and Revenue sentences, so which board's deadline it governs is ambiguous. The 61 Pa. Code 119.10 regulation also uses 90 days for the reassessment petition.
designImplication: For PA, the player can contest the tax within 90 days of a PIT assessment. A lien filed by mistake goes to a phone contact or the advocate, with no deadline and no guaranteed outcome.

claim: Pennsylvania DOR's PIT payment-plan page sets a standard plan as under 12 months and under $50,000. Longer or larger balances, or a second plan, need an extended plan. The page says nothing about liens. DOR's online answer center, seen only through search-result excerpts, says 'Payment plans do not stop the possibility of liens and federal offsets from occurring,' and that default can lead to liens, garnishment and other enforcement. No source says a lien is withheld or released while a plan is current, or that a plan requires a lien. The Fiscal Code allows installment compromises of up to seven years provided 'the security be not impaired'.

DOR answer center (https://revenue-pa.custhelp.com/app/answers/detail/a_id/4214/~/can-i-get-a-payment-plan-for-my-personal-income-taxes), per search excerpt: 'Payment plans do not stop the possibility of liens and federal offsets from occurring.' Fiscal Code s. 1409 (https://www.palegis.us/statutes/unconsolidated/law-information/view-statute?txtType=PDF&SessYr=1929&SessInd=0&ActNum=0176.&chpt=14&subchpt=000.&sctn=9&subsctn=000.): instalment compromise allowed 'Provided, That the amount of the debt be not lessened, and that the security be not impaired, and that the principal, with interest, together with costs, if any, be paid within seven years'.

It was seen only as search-engine excerpts, not read directly. Whether PA requires a lien for extended plans is NOT FOUND. Whether s. 1409 applies to PIT payment plans as administered today is not confirmed.
