claim: A Pennsylvania tax lien is a public court record docketed in the county prothonotary's office. DOR also publishes every state tax lien it files on the monthly 'Pennsylvania Tax Lien Publication List' in myPATH, showing the original lien amount. DOR says the lien makes the Commonwealth 'a priority creditor that must be paid before other financial transactions can take place (home sales, business transfer, obtaining a loan, etc.).' By statute it ranks ahead of later claims at judicial sale, subject to earlier-recorded mortgages and liens, sale costs and real estate taxes. DOR's enforcement list includes denying a tax clearance certificate needed for some licenses and contracts, and denying or revoking DOR-issued licenses. Those are tied to unpaid tax, not to the lien itself.

namedEffects: priority creditor before home sales, business transfer, obtaining a loan
priority at judicial sale over later claims (subject to prior recorded mortgages/liens, sale costs, real estate taxes)
writ of execution may issue directly on the lien

sourceDate: DOR PA Tax Liens page undated; REV-554 04-25; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: DOR page: 'When a lien is filed, it becomes a matter of public record. The lien ensures the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania is listed as a priority creditor that must be paid before other financial transactions can take place (home sales, business transfer, obtaining a loan, etc.).' 'The Pennsylvania Tax Lien Publication List is a resource that lists all state tax liens' and 'The list is updated monthly'. 'Liens, along with most other court records, are public documents.' TRC s. 345(b): liens 'shall have priority to, and be fully paid before, any other obligation ... subject, however, to mortgage or other liens existing and duly recorded at the time such tax lien is recorded'; 'A writ of execution may directly issue upon such lien'. REV-554 lists DOR actions: 'Disclose, by publication or otherwise, the taxpayer's name ... and tax balances as a result of a lien recorded', 'Deny a tax clearance certificate to a taxpayer applying for or requesting renewal of certain licenses, contracts, grants', 'Deny or revoke a license issued by the department.'
uncertainty: A statute that blocks title transfer outright is NOT FOUND; the 'must be paid before' language is DOR's description of priority. Which licenses require PA tax clearance was not researched. Credit effects were deliberately not researched; DOR's page discusses credit bureaus, but those statements are not used.
designImplication: In PA, a lien should publicly list the player's name and original amount each month, and a home sale, business transfer or new loan should have to pay it first. License or tax-clearance denial should be a separate unpaid-tax consequence.

claim: Ohio's income tax lien is not automatic on assessment. The assessment becomes final if no petition for reassessment is filed within 60 days of service. The Department of Taxation then certifies the unpaid assessment to the Attorney General for collection. A certified copy of the commissioner's final entry may then be filed with the clerk of the court of common pleas, and the clerk enters a judgment that has the same effect as other judgments. No minimum dollar threshold was found.

value.filedBy: Tax commissioner / Attorney General (certified copy of final assessment entry)
value.filedWith: Clerk of the court of common pleas

establishes: R.C. 5747.13: unless a petition for reassessment is filed "within sixty days after service of the notice of assessment" the assessment "becomes final". After that, "a certified copy of the tax commissioner's entry making the assessment final may be filed in the office of the clerk of the court of common pleas", and "the clerk shall enter a judgment against the party assessed" that "shall have the same effect as other judgments." ODT Assessments FAQ (dated May 15, 2020; read from an archive.org capture of 2023-01-31 at https://web.archive.org/web/20230131061452/https://tax.ohio.gov/help-center/faqs/assessments/assessments because the live page now returns 404): "If a balance due remains 60 days after receipt of the assessment, and you do not file an appeal, the Attorney General's Office will begin collection proceedings" and "when an assessment is forwarded to the Attorney General's Office for collection, a judgment lien is filed with the county clerk of courts."
uncertainty: Minimum dollar threshold: NOT FOUND (R.C. 5747.13 states none). The statute says the entry "may" be filed, so filing is discretionary. The exact gap between AG referral and the clerk filing is NOT FOUND. The ODT FAQ is from 2020 and now survives only as an archive copy, since the live URL returns 404.
designImplication: Model Ohio's lien as a step that follows a final assessment, at the earliest 60 days after the assessment notice and only once the debt goes to the Attorney General. An assessment that is merely unpaid should not by itself create a lien.

claim: No pre-filing notice of intent to lien, under a name of its own, was found for Ohio. The warning before referral is the notice of assessment itself, which ODT sends by certified mail. The Attorney General says this certified letter warns that the debt goes to the Attorney General if it is not resolved within 60 days. Once filed, the judgment lien follows from that referral.
sourceDate: page undated; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Ohio AG Tax FAQs: "The Ohio Department of Taxation sent you a certified letter advising that the debt would be turned over to the Attorney General if not resolved within 60 days from the date of the letter." R.C. 5747.13 (https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-5747.13) gives 60 days after service of the notice of assessment to petition for reassessment. ODT FAQ (2020; archive capture): "The Attorney General will issue a notice to you after they receive the tax claim."
uncertainty: A notice of intent to file a lien under its own name: NOT FOUND. Form number of the notice of assessment: NOT FOUND. The ODT notice-of-assessment sample PDF (tax.ohio.gov/static/self_help/atas0037noticeofassessment.pdf) returned 404. The name and timing of the AG's own notice after it receives the claim: NOT FOUND.
designImplication: Use the certified notice of assessment as the only warning: one notice, then a 60-day window, then AG referral and a judgment lien. Do not invent a separate intent-to-lien letter for Ohio.

claim: The judgment is entered by the clerk of the court of common pleas of the county. R.C. 5747.13 has the clerk enter it in a loose-leaf book titled 'special judgments for state and school district income taxes'. Ohio's general judgment-lien statute says the clerk's filing, docketing and indexing fee is taxed as costs of the judgment and included in the lien. No dollar amount was found, and no source confirmed that this general rule applies to 5747.13 tax judgments.

value.recordedWith: Clerk of the court of common pleas (county)
value.book: special judgments for state and school district income taxes

establishes: R.C. 5747.13: the clerk files the judgment "in one of two loose-leaf books, one entitled 'special judgments for state and school district income taxes'". R.C. 2329.02 (https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-2329.02, effective 2024-10-24) says of certificates of judgment generally: "The fee for such filing, docketing, and indexing shall be taxed as increased costs of such judgment ... and shall be included in the lien of the judgment." R.C. 109.081 (https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-109.081, effective 2017-04-06): "Up to eleven per cent" of amounts the AG collects "shall be assessed as a collection cost" and is "fully recoverable from the party indebted". AG Collections FAQ (https://ohioattorneygeneral.gov/FAQ/Collections-Enforcement): "Collection costs are added by statute (Ohio Revised Code section 109.081)."
uncertainty: Dollar amount of the clerk's filing fee for a 5747.13 judgment: NOT FOUND. Whether R.C. 2329.02's fee-as-costs rule applies to the 5747.13 special judgment book: NOT FOUND (that is an inference). The 11% is the AG's collection cost on everything it collects; it is not a lien filing fee, and the actual percentage set under the 'up to' cap was NOT FOUND.
designImplication: Treat the 11% AG collection cost as the main add-on once a debt is certified. Leave the lien filing fee at zero or null until a clerk fee is sourced.

claim: Once docketed, the tax judgment has the same effect as other judgments. Under R.C. 2329.02 a judgment becomes a lien on the debtor's lands and tenements in the county where the certificate of judgment is filed. Under R.C. 2329.07, a judgment in favor of the state becomes dormant and stops operating as a lien after 10 years from the judgment or its last renewal, or 15 years from the last execution, whichever is later. Execution, a filed certificate of judgment, garnishment or proceedings in aid of execution keep it alive.

value.attachesTo: lands and tenements of the judgment debtor in the county where filed

establishes: R.C. 2329.07: "a judgment in favor of the state, is dormant and shall not operate as a lien" unless, within 10 years from the judgment or renewal or 15 years from the last execution (whichever is later), "An execution on the judgment is issued", "A certificate of judgment is issued and filed", a garnishment order is issued, or proceedings in aid of execution are commenced. R.C. 2329.02 (https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-2329.02): a judgment "shall be a lien upon lands and tenements of each judgment debtor within any county of this state from the time there is filed in the office of the clerk of the court of common pleas of such county a certificate of such judgment". R.C. 5747.13: the judgment "shall have the same effect as other judgments."
uncertainty: No source found says outright that 2329.02 and 2329.07 govern a 5747.13 tax judgment. This entry infers it from 5747.13's 'same effect as other judgments'. Whether the lien reaches personal property: NOT FOUND.
designImplication: Model Ohio's lien as county-specific and limited to real estate. It lasts 10 years and is kept alive by collection activity. A character with no Ohio real estate feels the judgment mostly through collection (offset, garnishment), not through the lien.

claim: After payment the Attorney General sends the lien release to the debtor, and the debtor has to file it with the county officials (Clerk of Courts and/or County Recorder). The AG holds lien releases for 14 days when payment is by personal check or online ACH. No statutory deadline for issuing the release, and no release fee, was found.
sourceDate: page undated; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: AG Collections FAQ: "Lien releases are sent to debtors and it is their responsibility to file the releases with the appropriate county officials, such as the Clerk of Courts and/or the County Recorder." AG Collections page (https://www.ohioattorneygeneral.gov/Business/Collections): "there is a 14 day hold on lien releases for payments made via personal check/ACH online". Regional offices offer "Pick up lien releases/duplicate lien releases".
uncertainty: Days from full payment to release for cash or certified funds: NOT FOUND. Fee to record the release: NOT FOUND. A process for releasing an erroneous filing: NOT FOUND. These are AG pages; no statute on release timing was found.
designImplication: After an Ohio payoff, the release reaches the character, and the lien stays on record until the character files it. Add a 14-day wait when they pay by check or ACH.

claim: The statutory route against an Ohio income tax assessment is a written petition for reassessment within 60 days after service of the notice of assessment. If the corrected assessment is less than what was paid, the overpayment is refunded. No Ohio procedure for challenging a judgment lien itself as filed in error was found. For AG-held debts, the AG says it considers evidence of identity theft case by case.
establishes: R.C. 5747.13: "Unless the party assessed files with the tax commissioner within sixty days after service of the notice of assessment a written petition for reassessment ... the assessment becomes final"; "If upon final determination of the petition an error in the assessment is corrected ... there shall be issued ... a refund". AG Collections FAQ (https://ohioattorneygeneral.gov/FAQ/Collections-Enforcement): "In cases of claimed identity theft, the agency/university will consider the evidence ... Each case is considered on an individual basis." AG Tax FAQ (https://www.ohioattorneygeneral.gov/faq/department-of-taxation-accounts): the AG asks for copies of what was sent to ODT "in order to justify ceasing collection efforts until the Department of Taxation has made a determination."
uncertainty: A procedure and deadline for correcting or vacating a judgment lien filed in error: NOT FOUND. R.C. 5747.13 does not address it. The AG Application for Administrative Review form was fetched but could not be read (binary PDF), and from its search listing it appears to concern refund offsets, not liens.
designImplication: Let a character contest the Ohio assessment in its 60-day window. After the lien is filed, an error should be resolved through ODT, which pauses AG collection, rather than through a dedicated lien-dispute action.

claim: ODT itself cannot set up payment plans. A plan is available only after the account is referred to the Attorney General, and that referral is the same step at which the judgment lien is filed. So an Ohio payment plan does not prevent the lien. The AG can agree to installment plans of up to one year, which require meeting a representative and signing a payment contract. No source says the lien is released while a plan is current.
sourceDate: ODT FAQ dated May 15, 2020 (archive.org capture 2023-01-31; live page returns 404); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: ODT Assessments FAQ: "Ohio law does not authorize the Department of Taxation to set up a payment plan"; "partial payments will not stop the imposition of additional interest or the referral of the account to the Attorney General's Office"; "To arrange for a payment plan, you must wait until we refer your account to the Attorney General's Office"; "The Attorney General's Office can accept your request for installment payments and agree to payment plans of up to one year. You will be required to meet with a representative ... and to sign a payment contract." Same FAQ: "when an assessment is forwarded to the Attorney General's Office for collection, a judgment lien is filed". AG Collections FAQ (https://ohioattorneygeneral.gov/FAQ/Collections-Enforcement): "The system is being updated. Currently, if you are trying to pay after your due date the system will ask for balance in full."
uncertainty: The one-year plan limit comes from a 2020 FAQ that survives only as an archive capture, so it may be out of date. Whether a lien is released or withheld while a plan is current: NOT FOUND. That a plan does not stop the lien is an inference from the sequence (plan only after referral; lien at referral).
designImplication: In Ohio, put the lien ahead of any payment plan: a character who wants installments has already been referred and is already under a judgment lien. Cap plans at 12 months, and let a plan only stop further collection, never remove the lien.

claim: Ohio's tax judgment lien is a public record, filed with the county clerk of courts. ODT says it does not report to the credit bureaus but that anyone can obtain the public record. A filed judgment lets the state levy execution, and once the debt is certified the AG adds collection costs and may offset refunds. No Ohio license denial, title-transfer block or priority rule tied specifically to this lien was found.
sourceDate: ODT FAQ dated May 15, 2020 (archive.org capture 2023-01-31); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: ODT FAQ: "a judgment lien is filed with the county clerk of courts. This information is public record." R.C. 5747.13 (https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-5747.13): "Execution shall issue upon the judgment upon the request of the tax commissioner". AG Tax FAQ (https://www.ohioattorneygeneral.gov/faq/department-of-taxation-accounts): "Your federal and/or state refunds are subject to offset when it is determined a tax debt is owed and has been turned over to the Attorney General for collection."
uncertainty: Ohio license denial or suspension for unpaid individual income tax: NOT FOUND (not searched exhaustively). A statutory priority rule for the 5747.13 judgment: NOT FOUND. Credit effects were deliberately not researched.
designImplication: Show the Ohio lien as a public record and as the trigger for execution and refund offset. Do not attach license or vehicle-title penalties, because no source supports them.

claim: By statute, the DC tax lien arises when a person neglects or refuses to pay after demand. It is deemed to arise at assessment, or on the return due date if the return was not filed on time. OTR says a lien may be filed with the Recorder of Deeds if the taxpayer does not pay within 10 days after receiving a Notice of Tax Due and a demand for payment. No minimum balance for filing was found, except in the installment-agreement context (see lien-payment-plan).

value.automaticOnAssessment: statutory lien arises at assessment after demand; filing is separate
value.arisesAt: assessment date, or return due date if return not timely filed

sourceDate: page undated; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: OTR Enforcement Actions: "A tax lien may be filed with the District of Columbia Recorder of Deeds if a taxpayer neglects or refuses to pay the District within 10 days after receiving a Notice of Tax Due and a demand for payment." D.C. Code § 47-4421(a) (https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/code/sections/47-4421): "If a person liable to pay a tax neglects or refuses to pay the tax after demand, the amount ... shall be a lien in favor of the District of Columbia". § 47-4422 (https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/code/sections/47-4422): the lien "shall be deemed to have arisen at the time the assessment is made, or if the tax return is not timely filed, on the due date of the tax return".
uncertainty: A dollar threshold for filing outside an installment agreement: NOT FOUND. The statute contains no 10-day period; it comes from the OTR page only.
designImplication: For DC, give the District a lien at assessment, but publish it only if the Notice of Tax Due goes unpaid for 10 days. The secret lien and the recorded lien should be separate states.

claim: DC sends a Notice of Tax, Penalty and/or Interest Due. If full payment is not received within 15 days of the notice date, OTR sends a Notice of Enforcement by certified mail and begins enforcement. OTR's lien page refers to the Notice of Tax Due and demand for payment, with a 10-day window before a lien may be filed. A 10% collection fee applies to balances unpaid 90 days or more and is avoided by paying within 30 days of a Notice of Enforcement Action. No notice titled as an intent to lien, and no form numbers, were found.

value.noticeName: Notice of Tax, Penalty and/or Interest Due; then Notice of Enforcement (certified mail)

sourceDate: page undated; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: OTR Notice of Tax Due: "If a tax is not fully paid, a Notice of Tax, Penalty and/or Interest Due will be mailed"; "If full payment is not received within 15 days from the notice date, the Office of Tax and Revenue (OTR) will send a Notice of Enforcement by certified mail, and the OTR will initiate enforcement action". OTR Enforcement Actions (https://otr.cfo.dc.gov/page/enforcement-actions): lien may be filed "within 10 days after receiving a Notice of Tax Due and a demand for payment". OTR Collections & Audit FAQs (https://otr.cfo.dc.gov/page/collections-audit-faqs): "a collection fee (also known as an O-Type Fee) of 10 percent on all unpaid balances that are owed for a period of 90 days or more. Taxpayers may avoid the fee by paying amounts due within 30 days of a Notice of Enforcement Action."
uncertainty: Form numbers of both notices: NOT FOUND. OTR's pages give two different windows (10 days before a lien may be filed; 15 days before a Notice of Enforcement), and it is NOT FOUND whether a lien is filed only after the Notice of Enforcement. A dedicated notice of intent to lien: NOT FOUND.
designImplication: Chain DC's notices: Notice of Tax Due, then about 10–15 days, then Notice of Enforcement by certified mail, with a lien possible after that. Add the 10% fee at 90 days unless the character pays within 30 days of the enforcement notice.

claim: DC files its tax liens with the District's Recorder of Deeds, where they become public record. OTR also says it files the lien in county courthouses across the country wherever the taxpayer has assets. No fee charged to the taxpayer for recording the lien was found.

value.recordedWith: District of Columbia Recorder of Deeds; also out-of-District county courthouses where assets are located

sourceDate: page undated; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: OTR Collections & Audit FAQs: "The lien is recorded at the District's Recorder of Deeds (ROD) office, where the information becomes public record"; "OTR will also file the tax lien in county courthouse(s) throughout the country where assets are located". D.C. Code § 47-4423(a) (https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/code/sections/47-4423): the lien is not valid against purchasers and others "until the lien has been filed with the Recorder of Deeds." The lien covers "any costs that may accrue" (§ 47-4421(a)).
uncertainty: Whether the taxpayer is charged a recording fee, and how much: NOT FOUND. The ROD FAQ (https://otr.cfo.dc.gov/page/rod-faqs) links a general 'New Fee Structure' PDF that was not read. § 47-4421's lien covers accrued 'costs', but no source says recording costs are passed on.
designImplication: Record DC liens at the Recorder of Deeds, and let them reach assets elsewhere through out-of-District filings. Charge no recording fee unless one is sourced.

claim: The DC lien attaches to all of the person's property and rights to property, real and personal, including property acquired while the lien lasts, and it has the same effect as a judgment lien. It continues until the liability or a resulting judgment is satisfied or becomes unenforceable. Collection by levy or court proceeding must begin within 10 years after assessment, and the taxpayer and the Mayor may extend that period in writing. No refiling requirement was found.

value.attachesTo: all property and rights to property, real and personal, including after-acquired property
value.durationBasis: until satisfied or unenforceable; collection limited to 10 years after assessment (D.C. Code 47-4302)
value.renewable: by written agreement extending the collection period

sourceDate: D.C. Code as published on code.dccouncil.gov, last amended 2007 (D.C. Law 16-205); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: § 47-4421(a): a lien "upon all property (including rights to property), whether real or personal, belonging to the person, and shall have the same effect as a lien created by judgment. The lien shall attach to all property ... belonging to, or acquired by, the person at any time during the period of the lien." § 47-4422 (https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/code/sections/47-4422): it "shall continue until the liability for the amount assessed (or a judgment against the taxpayer arising out of the liability) is satisfied or becomes unenforceable". § 47-4302 (https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/code/sections/47-4302): collection by levy or court proceeding only if "begun within 10 years after the assessment"; the period may be extended if "both the Mayor and the taxpayer have consented in writing". OTR Installment Agreements page: "The taxpayer agrees to extend the statute of limitations for collection until the final payment is paid."
uncertainty: No DC section says outright that the lien ends at 10 years. That is inferred from 'becomes unenforceable' read with the 10-year collection limit in § 47-4302 (with suspensions under § 47-4303). Whether a recorded lien must be refiled: NOT FOUND.
designImplication: Make DC's lien a blanket claim on everything the character owns or later acquires, ending when the debt is paid or the 10-year collection window closes. Signing a payment plan should extend that window.

claim: OTR says a lien can be released when a District real estate sale pays the tax from its proceeds. No DC statute or OTR page was found that states how long after full payment the lien release issues, whether the taxpayer must request it, or whether a release fee applies. The release statute found, § 47-4478, covers levies, not liens.
sourceDate: page undated; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: OTR Enforcement Actions: "If the taxpayer attempts to sell real estate in the District, the taxes due will be paid out of the sale proceeds, at which time the lien can be released." Same page, on offsets: "Once the liability has been paid in full, the levy will be released." D.C. Code § 47-4478 (https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/code/sections/47-4478) requires release of a LEVY when the liability "is satisfied or becomes unenforceable" or under an installment agreement; it does not address liens.
uncertainty: Release timing, the request procedure, release fee, and release for an erroneous filing: all NOT FOUND. The collection-issues FAQ (otr.cfo.dc.gov/book/other-topics-faqs/collection-issues) returned 403. A law-firm page (alexanderpowell.law, SECONDARY) and a tax-relief page (SECONDARY, not cited) give no sourced release timing.
designImplication: Release a DC lien on full payment, including payoff at a property sale. Keep the timing as a placeholder flag, not a number of days, until OTR is sourced.

claim: No DC procedure specific to a lien filed in error was found. The general OTR collection-decision route is a written protest to the Collection and Enforcement Administration, with a response within 30 calendar days. Reconsideration may be requested within 30 days of that response and is answered within 120 days. After that the taxpayer may go to the Taxpayer Advocate, or to Superior Court within six months of the assessment, paying in full first. Protests of non-filer assessments go to the Office of Administrative Hearings.
sourceDate: page undated; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: OTR 'How Do I Request Reconsideration of a Decision (CEA)': "Once OTR receives your request, a response will be issued to you within 30 calendar days"; "you have 30 days from the response date to request a reconsideration"; "You will receive a response to your reconsideration request within 120 days"; "you can appeal your decision to the Superior Court ... within six (6) months from the date of the assessment. Please note: the tax, penalty and interest must be paid in full before the expiration of the six-month period." "protest regarding Officer Assessments and Non-Filer assessments must be submitted the Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH)". Its listed examples are penalty waivers, offers in compromise and refund offsets, not liens.
uncertainty: A lien-specific error or withdrawal process and its deadlines: NOT FOUND. Whether this CEA process covers a disputed lien: NOT FOUND (inferred only). DC Code §§ 47-4421 to 47-4423 contain no release-for-error provision.
designImplication: Send a DC lien dispute through the general CEA protest: a decision in about 30 days, a further 30 days to seek reconsideration, then up to 120 days for that answer. Court review requires paying first.

claim: DC files a lien automatically when an installment agreement has a balance over $25,000. For smaller balances it files one when the plan runs longer than 12 months. So some plans require a lien and others are made without one. Self-service plans are limited to 24 months and balances under $100,000, need a 10% down payment and ACH, and extend the collection statute. If the plan is defaulted or cancelled, 'a lien could be filed'. No source says an existing lien is released while a plan is current.

value.lienWithheldDuringPlan: only if balance <= 25000 and plan <= 12 months

sourceDate: page undated; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: OTR Installment Agreements: "LIEN DETERMINATION An automatic lien will be filed if the installment agreement has: A balance greater than $25,000.00; If the balance is less than $25,000.00, a lien will be filed if the length of the plan is greater than 12 months." "The length of the payment plan is 24 months or less Balance is under $100,000.00"; "10% Down payment"; "ACH is required"; "or the agreement will be cancelled. A lien could be filed"; "The taxpayer agrees to extend the statute of limitations for collection until the final payment is paid." "installment agreements are not required by law, however the Office of Tax and Revenue may extend agreements as a courtesy."
uncertainty: Release of an existing lien while a plan is current: NOT FOUND. Behavior at exactly $25,000 is not stated (the page says 'greater than' and 'less than'). D.C. Code § 47-4478 requires a LEVY (not a lien) to be released under an installment agreement.
designImplication: Make DC's lien a cost of a long or large payment plan: balance over $25,000 or term over 12 months means a lien is filed. A short, small plan avoids it, and a default reopens the lien.

claim: A recorded DC tax lien is public record at the Recorder of Deeds. OTR says it gives the District a preferred claim over other creditors, can prevent borrowing or selling real estate, enables seizure of property, can appear in newspapers and business journals, and is displayed on OTR's website. Separately, DC's Clean Hands law bars issuing or reissuing a DC license or permit to anyone owing more than $1,000 in past-due taxes or who has failed to file required returns. It does not apply while a timely appeal is pending or while the person is complying with an agreed payment schedule.

value.priority: preferred claim over other creditors once filed (valid against purchasers etc. only after filing with Recorder of Deeds)
value.blocksTitleTransfer: can prevent borrowing or selling real estate; paid from sale proceeds

sourceDate: page undated; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: OTR Collections & Audit FAQs: "A filed tax lien enables the District to seize property"; "Since tax liens become public record, they can appear in local newspapers and business journals ... in addition to being displayed on the OTR's website." OTR Enforcement Actions (https://otr.cfo.dc.gov/page/enforcement-actions): "The tax lien puts the public on notice that the District has a preferred claim over other creditors"; it "can prevent them from borrowing money or selling real estate." D.C. Code § 47-4423(a): not valid against a bona fide purchaser, security-interest holder, mechanic's lienor or judgment lien creditor "until the lien has been filed with the Recorder of Deeds." D.C. Code § 47-2862 (https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/code/sections/47-2862): no license or permit if the applicant "Owes the District more than $1,000 in past due taxes" or "Has failed to file required District tax returns"; (b) excepts a pending timely appeal; (c) excepts compliance with an agreed payment schedule. OTR Clean Hands FAQs (https://otr.cfo.dc.gov/page/clean-hands-faqs): someone on a payment plan can still get a Certificate of Clean Hands once the down payment posts and payments are current.
uncertainty: The Clean Hands bar is triggered by the tax debt, not by the lien itself. The $1,000 figure is the statute as currently published (an older $100 figure appears only for DMV debts in (a-1)). Credit effects were deliberately not researched.
designImplication: Have a DC tax debt over $1,000 block licenses and permits through Clean Hands whether or not a lien is filed, and have a current payment plan lift the block. Once filed, the lien marks the character's real estate as unsellable without payoff.

claim: In Oklahoma, unpaid tax is a statutory lien from the date it is due (68 O.S. 234). Separately, if a tax is not paid before it becomes delinquent, the Tax Commission 'may immediately issue a warrant' and must at once file it with the county clerk, where the filing is notice of the state's lien on the taxpayer's real property (68 O.S. 231). For an assessed income tax, the proposed assessment becomes final if not protested within 60 days, and OTC rules say a warrant 'shall be issued' if the taxpayer neither protests nor pays within the time allowed. No dollar threshold was found.

value.automaticOnAssessment: statutory lien from due date (68 O.S. 234); filed warrant lien after delinquency

sourceDate: Title 68 compilation from oklegislature.gov, includes amendments effective through July 1, 2026; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: 68 O.S. § 231(A): "If any tax ... is not paid before the same becomes delinquent, the Oklahoma Tax Commission may immediately issue a warrant under its official seal." § 231(B): "The Tax Commission shall, immediately upon issuance of the warrant, file with the county clerk ... a copy thereof". § 234(A): taxes "constitute a lien in favor of the state upon all franchises, property, and rights to property ... from the date the taxes are due and payable". § 221(C),(E): protest "Within sixty (60) days after the date indicated on the aforesaid proposed assessment"; otherwise it "shall become final and absolute." OAC 710:50 (https://oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/tax/documents/resources/rules-and-policies/agency-rules/2024/Chapter_50_Income_2024.pdf): "In the event the taxpayer does not protest this assessment or pay the taxes due within the time allowed, a tax warrant shall be issued. [See: 68 O.S. § 221]" (this rule is in the withholding/non-filer context). OTC Tax Warrants page (https://oklahoma.gov/tax/helpcenter/taxwarrants.html): "filed ... when state taxes remain unpaid after the taxes become delinquent."
uncertainty: A minimum amount before a warrant issues: NOT FOUND. The number of days after a final assessment before a warrant is in practice issued: NOT FOUND (the statute says 'may immediately'). OSCN, the official statute site, blocked automated access, so the statute text was read from the Legislature's own full-title PDF.

claim: No Oklahoma notice of intent to file a tax warrant, by any name, was found. The steps before a warrant are the proposed assessment (60 days to protest) and, for a balance due on a filed return, a billing notice. The statute requires the OTC to mail a copy of the warrant to the taxpayer's last-known address immediately when it issues, which is notice after the fact, not before.

claim: The OTC files the tax warrant electronically with the county clerk, who records and indexes it in the same manner as judgments. The OTC may recover from the taxpayer any fee the county clerk charges for filing a tax lien or warrant. One county clerk (Washington County) lists $8 to file an Oklahoma tax warrant and $8 to release one. A separate statutory additional penalty of $15, or 10% of the warrant up to $200 (whichever is greater), is imposed on each delinquent tax debtor as a collection fee.

claim: The filed warrant is notice of the state's lien on any interest in the taxpayer's real property in that county. It is paramount to liens that attach later, and is in addition to the general statutory lien of 68 O.S. 234, which covers all franchises, property and rights to property, real or personal, including after-acquired property. The lien is released on payment, or ends 10 years after the warrant was filed, unless the OTC refiles before then. A refiled warrant continues the lien for 10 years from refiling. A filed warrant is not subject to any dormancy statute.

value.attachesTo: filed warrant: taxpayer's real property in the county; statutory lien (234): all franchises, property and rights to property, real or personal, including after-acquired

sourceDate: Title 68 compilation, amendments through July 1, 2026; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: 68 O.S. § 231(B): filing "shall constitute and be evidence and notice of the state's lien upon any interest in any real property of the taxpayer"; the lien "shall be paramount and superior to all other liens ... attaching to any of said property subsequent to the date and time of such filing"; "released and extinguished upon the payment ... or ... upon the expiration of ten (10) years after the date upon which the warrant was filed"; "the Tax Commission may, prior to the release and extinguishment of such lien, refile the warrant"; a refiled warrant continues the lien "upon the expiration of ten (10) years after the date upon which the warrant was refiled". § 231(I)(2): "Not be subject to the provisions of any dormancy statute". § 234(A): lien on "all franchises, property, and rights to property, whether real or personal, then belonging to or thereafter acquired".

designImplication: Let an Oklahoma warrant lien last 10 years and let the state renew it before then. A character cannot simply wait it out if the OTC keeps refiling.

claim: Only the Commission can release a tax warrant, and only after its Income Tax Accounts Division determines that the tax, penalty and interest to date, and all statutory penalties and fees, are paid in full. Warrants are not fully released unless paid in full. A partial release can remove the lien from one specific property: there is no application fee, but an offer is expected, typically 10% of the warrant or $500, whichever is more. A release for no consideration is issued when the lien clouds title because of an error in the property description or a similarity of names. No number of days after payment for the release was found.

(2) The penalty imposed by law and all other fees authorized by law have been paid in full." OAC 710:1-3-56: if the face amount is paid directly, the Commission determines "whether the collection fee has attached and either release the warrant, or request the sheriff to pursue additional collection efforts". OTC Tax Warrants page (https://oklahoma.gov/tax/helpcenter/taxwarrants.html): "Tax warrants are not fully released unless paid in full"; partial release: "There is not an application fee"; "Standard amount: 10% of the total tax warrant (including interest, penalties, and fees) or $500, whichever is more". 68 O.S. § 231.3 (os68.pdf): release "for no consideration after a determination ... that the lien or warrant is clouding the title of property by reason of an error in the description of such property or by reason of similarity of names."

claim: Questions about whether a tax warrant is valid (wrong name, wrong business, wrong address) go to the OTC's Income Tax Accounts Division. If a warrant clouds a property's title through an error in the property description or a similarity of names, the OTC releases it for no consideration and may recover its filing fee. The assessment itself can be protested within 60 days of the proposed assessment. After it becomes final, the taxpayer has one year to ask that it be adjusted or abated as clearly erroneous, but that request does not stay collection. No deadline for disputing the warrant itself was found.

claim: Individuals can set up an Oklahoma income tax payment plan on OkTAP using the Letter ID on their billing notice. No source was found saying whether a tax warrant is withheld, filed, or released while a plan is current. What was found: the OTC lists warrant holders over $25,000 and more than 90 days delinquent as 'Top 100' delinquents, and tells them to contact the Tax Warrant Section 'to make payment arrangements', so plans can exist alongside filed warrants. For licensees, a taxpayer abiding by a payment agreement is deemed in compliance under 68 O.S. 238.1.

The Letter ID from the billing letter you received will give you access to set up a payment plan." Same page, Top 100: "persons who owe delinquent taxes ... in excess of $25,000 which are unpaid for more than 90 days and for which a tax warrant has been filed"; they "should contact the Oklahoma Tax Commission, Tax Warrant Section ... to make payment arrangements." 68 O.S. § 238.1(D) (os68.pdf): "A licensee who has entered into and is abiding by a payment agreement ... shall be deemed to be in compliance". OAC 710:1-3-54 permits release only on payment in full.

claim: An Oklahoma tax warrant filed with the county clerk is a public record, and the OTC keeps a monthly register of outstanding warrants open to inspection. The OTC publishes a 'Top 100' list of delinquents owing over $25,000, unpaid more than 90 days, with a warrant filed. It says a lien means the owner cannot sell or refinance the property without addressing it, that it must be paid or released at closing, that it appears on title searches, and that the state has priority over most other debts. The filed warrant also gives the OTC all the collection remedies of a district court judgment, including levy and sale. For licensees out of compliance, 68 O.S. 238.1 leads to garnishment, and the Bar Association begins suspension proceedings for attorneys.
